title: The earth
hook: don't waste, don't destroy, care for the land
tomorrow: Noa's cat-sitting for Mr. Feld. is the rule about the cat, or her?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the porters, the broken barrels, and Rav: give back the cloaks, and pay them. Pay today. People aren't the only thing the Torah says not to wear down.

After the last show comes strike, and a whole set goes into a dumpster: painted flats, a staircase, a door that opened every night. Now an odd line. In the middle of the Torah's laws of war, a city under siege, the text stops to talk about trees. Don't cut down the fruit trees, it says. Then it asks a strange question, in the JPS 1917 translation: "for is the tree of the field man, that it should be besieged of thee?"
screen: `THE SET GOES IN A DUMPSTER.` → `A SIEGE, AND THEN TREES.` → `"IS THE TREE OF THE FIELD MAN?"`

segments.voice: So why does a war law stop for trees? Part of the answer is in the question. The tree isn't your enemy. It can't run behind the walls, and it didn't start this. Even at war there's a line: you don't destroy what feeds people just because you can. The rabbis carried that line out of the battlefield and into the house. They called it bal tashchit, do not destroy, and the Talmud stretches it to things like wasting a lamp's oil or ruining good clothes for no reason. Then a second verse widens it again. About the land, God says in Leviticus: "for the land is Mine." The people living on it are tenants, sharing it with each other and with whoever comes next. A midrash makes it tender. God walks Adam through the garden and shows him the trees: see how beautiful they are. Take care not to ruin My world, because if you ruin it, there is no one to repair it after you. Lived, the earth looks ordinary: the set flats reused for the next show, the shoes resoled, the leftovers eaten, the faucet off while you brush. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Torah's rule against waste starts in the middle of a war.
screen: `THE TREE ISN'T YOUR ENEMY.` · `BAL TASHCHIT: DO NOT DESTROY.` · `FOR THE LAND IS MINE.` · `DON'T RUIN MY WORLD.` · then, large: `THE LAND IS SHARED.`

segments.voice: Pick up one thing near you that's headed for the trash: a jar, a box, a half-used notebook. Turn it over in your hands for a few slow breaths. Ask it the Torah's kind of question: is it finished, or only finished for me?
screen: `ONE THING HEADED FOR THE TRASH.` · `TURN IT OVER.` · `FINISHED, OR ONLY FOR ME?`

segments.voice: The earth: a world on loan, with a line even war doesn't cross. Don't destroy what can still give.
Worth keeping: the land is shared, with your neighbors and with whoever comes next. Nine of twenty.

screen: `DAY 1731 COUNTS.` → `COMMUNITY AND JUSTICE · 9 OF 20.` → `TOMORROW: IS THE RULE ABOUT THE CAT, OR HER?`

howItsDone: Many Jews cite bal tashchit, the rule against needless destruction, when they talk about waste and the environment; Tu BiShvat, the new year for trees, is often marked with tree planting and care for the land.

pairs: not your enemy in a siege

myth: the Torah's rule about trees is set in peacetime
it's set in the middle of a siege: even at war, don't cut down the fruit trees.
the rabbis stretched bal tashchit past trees to other waste
the Talmud applies it to wasting lamp oil and ruining good clothes.
caring for the earth has no roots in the Torah itself
Deuteronomy protects the fruit trees, Leviticus says 'the land is Mine', and a midrash has God warning Adam not to ruin the world.

fork.reveal: the rabbis stretched the fruit-tree law to anything still useful. the question is whether it can still give, not whether it's a tree.

original.note: Hebrew: do not destroy; the rabbis' name for the rule against needless waste.

what it means: even at war, don't destroy what still gives life; the world is on loan to everyone.
what a scholar hears: Deuteronomy 20:19–20 becomes the rabbinic rule bal tashchit (Shabbat 67b, Kiddushin 32a), beside Leviticus 25:23 and Ecclesiastes Rabbah 7:13.

chat.says: after closing, the whole set goes in the dumpster. crew says "that's theater." am i being dramatic?
options: Not dramatic: bal tashchit means don't destroy what's still useful. Ask about reusing it.
Yes. The rule is about fruit trees in wartime, not painted plywood on a stage.
A little. It's only wasteful when the things you throw out belong to you.
chat.meaning: The rabbis stretched Deuteronomy's fruit-tree law into bal tashchit: don't destroy anything still useful. The land, and what it makes, is shared.

bal tashchit.meaning: do not destroy: the rule against needless waste

midrash.meaning: a rabbinic teaching that reads deeply into scripture

Talmud.meaning: the great collection of the rabbis' discussions and law

notes: Deuteronomy 20:19 and Leviticus 25:23 fragments quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording and punctuation.

Bal tashchit extended in the Talmud: Shabbat 67b (covering an oil lamp / uncovering a naphtha lamp, making it burn wastefully) and Kiddushin 32a (tearing garments). Summarized as 'wasting a lamp's oil or ruining good clothes for no reason'. Confirm both citations.
The reading 'the tree isn't your enemy' follows the verse's own question; confirm framing.
